claim: Novel reading fills young people with fantasy and unfits them for real, rational life.
what_happened: The novel became the dominant literary form and a staple of school curricula; the generation warned off it ran the culture.
lesson: When a medium is accused of making the young prefer an imaginary world, check whether the accusers are describing a harm or just a new taste.

quotes.text: They lead young people into an enchanted country, and open to their view an imaginary world
quotes.speaker: Augusta Herald (reprinted)

quotes.text: The evils of indiscriminate novel reading have been much dwelt upon.
quotes.speaker: John E. Edwards

claim: A confirmed novel reader becomes morbid and callous, all fine sentiment and no charitable action.
what_happened: Later research on literary fiction tends to find the opposite: reading fiction is associated with better theory of mind and empathy.
lesson: A claim that a new medium makes people feel less is testable; the novel was charged with numbing empathy and is now studied as a tool for building it.

quotes.text: A confirmed novel reader is always morbid; on some sides prelernaturally sensitive, on others preternaturally callous
quotes.speaker: O. A. Brownson

quotes.text: He who stops to sentimentalize about poverty, will be the last to throw his cloak over the tattered gabardine of the beggar.
quotes.speaker: O. A. Brownson

claim: Cheap sensational dime novels turn boys into thieves, highwaymen and murderers.
what_happened: Dime novels faded into nostalgia; by 1937 the press was lauding them and blaming movies instead, and later comics, TV and games inherited the charge.
lesson: Police and courts reaching for the newest medium to explain a crime is a recurring pattern; expect the blame to move on to the next format within a generation.

quotes.text: Three boys, readers of dime-novels, have gone to prison, one for life and the others for forty years each; .but the publisher of the dime-novel has hie liberty and doubtless much wealth.
quotes.speaker: The Atchison Tribune

quotes.text: I am satisfied that when we land him he will prove to be a pervert, whose mind has become unbalanced through reading dime novels and other trashy literature.
quotes.speaker: Captain of Detectives Seymour

quotes.text: Officials Say That the Dime Novel Habit is Eesponsible.
quotes.speaker: The Boston Globe

claim: Too much novel reading unbalances the mind and drives young people to suicide.
what_happened: No link between novel reading and suicide was ever established; the same story template was later applied to comics, rock music, games and social media.
lesson: An anecdote of one tragedy plus one habit is not a mechanism; a fear built only on such stories should be weighed far below one built on rates.

quotes.text: Cause of suicide, sentimental novels.
quotes.speaker: Courier-Post

quotes.text: He was, however, a groat reader of novels, and It Is believed his mind became affected from too much reading.
quotes.speaker: St. Louis Post-Dispatch

thing: Mass reading (cheap books and free libraries)
claim: Reading has become a craze and a narcotic, a dangerous stimulant that replaces thinking.
what_happened: Literacy and reading became the benchmark of a healthy mind; today the worry runs the other way, that people read too little.
lesson: Today's "dangerous stimulant" is often tomorrow's virtue that the next medium is accused of killing; don't stake a product thesis on yesterday's moral panic.

quotes.text: Reading is a kind of craze that has gotten hold of the people. It is a dangerous habit, like a stimulant.
quotes.speaker: Daniel Coit Gilman

quotes.text: Books have become the modern narcotic.
quotes.speaker: Buffalo Evening News

quotes.text: mental intoxication, consequent upon too great indulgence in the printed page, is as bad as physical intoxication.
quotes.speaker: Charles P. Donoghue

claim: Free libraries make children read too much, crowding their minds and hurting their schoolwork.
what_happened: Children's libraries became a civic standard and early reading a top predictor of school success.
lesson: A worry that kids get "too much" of a newly free resource usually reflects the novelty of access, as this writer half-admits, not lasting harm.

quotes.text: The tendency now is to read too much, but this may be caused by the novelty of getting any book whenever you want it
quotes.speaker: The Kansas State Register

quotes.text: Children Read Too Much!
quotes.speaker: Grand Island Independent

claim: Reading in bed ruins the eyes, strains the body, and is as bad a habit as taking drugs.
what_happened: The fire risk was real in the candle era (a reader burned to death in 1870) and vanished with electric light; the drug-like harm never appeared, though near work is linked to myopia.
lesson: Separate the hazard of the delivery method (a candle) from the activity itself (reading); fix the hazard and the activity survives.

quotes.text: the habit is as bad as taking drugs.
quotes.speaker: unnamed doctor (Daily Mail)

quotes.text: came by her death on Saturday through the dangerous praohce of reading in bed.
quotes.speaker: Daily News

quotes.text: Reading in Bed Strains the Eyes
quotes.speaker: The Call

claim: Reading in moving railway cars exhausts and damages the eyes.
what_happened: Reading on trains became the standard commuter habit; no lasting eye damage was found beyond motion discomfort.
lesson: Discomfort is not damage; a new habit that feels tiring at first can still become universal.

quotes.text: the constant motion and oscillations of the car render it impossible to hold the book in one position
quotes.speaker: a distinguished oculist

claim: There are too many books and periodicals; the result is distraction and mental indigestion.
what_happened: Output kept rising (Britain alone now publishes well over 100,000 titles a year) and readers learned to filter; the same complaint is now aimed at feeds and AI-generated content.
lesson: Abundance complaints are perennial; the opportunity is usually in filtering and curation, not in arguing for less supply.

quotes.text: the disease of the age was distraction, hurry, interest in far too many things, with the consequent result of mental indigestion
quotes.speaker: Professor Meiklejohn

quotes.text: For surely there can be no doubt about the matter; there are too many books.
quotes.speaker: Aldous Huxley

quotes.text: The existence of all these books created a restless spirit
quotes.speaker: R. K. Dent

claim: The bicycle craze is emptying libraries because people ride instead of reading.
what_happened: The bicycle boom collapsed around 1900 and library use kept growing; books and bikes coexisted.
lesson: A new pastime can dent an old one during its boom without killing it; measure after the craze peaks, not during it.

quotes.text: The bicycle is blamed for this literary defection.
quotes.speaker: The Union Leader

claim: Cheap postage and stationery have ended the art of the long, thoughtful letter.
what_happened: Letter volume exploded while the long letter shrank, the same trade later seen with telegrams, email and texting.
lesson: Cheaper communication makes each message shorter and the total far larger; that is a format shift, and businesses that ride the volume win.

quotes.text: there is too much writing scribbling going on, not only among Jane's class, but among her social betters.
quotes.speaker: a pessimistic observer (Philadelphia Times)

claim: A talented young woman is wasting her gifts by writing fiction instead of improving religious works.
what_happened: Augusta Evans's "Beulah" became a bestseller and she one of the most popular American novelists of the century.
lesson: Dismissing a creator because of the form they chose is a bet against where the audience already is.

quotes.text: we are sorry to know tha't she is was'ing the oinne talent in the cutii. position of the work of fiction.
quotes.speaker: Florence Gazette

claim: Giving children names taken from novels is an insult to Christianity and corrupts them.
what_happened: Names from fiction (Vanessa, Wendy, Pamela, later Arya) became ordinary.
lesson: Culture-war panics over small choices tend to look quaint fast; don't design around them.

quotes.text: How can parents ad monish their childrc-j against novel reading after they have lakes their uames from novels ?
quotes.speaker: Valley Spirit

claim: Excessive novel reading by idle married women is responsible for most divorces.
what_happened: Divorce rates tracked law, economics and women's independence, not reading habits.
lesson: When a single habit is blamed for a large social trend, look for the structural cause the critic is avoiding.

quotes.text: The Danger of Novel Reading
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Dix

claim: Current novels are obscene and must be submitted to the district attorney for banning.
what_happened: "Banned in Boston" became a selling point; Elmer Gantry is a classic and Sinclair Lewis won the Nobel Prize in 1930.
lesson: Censorship of a new work often becomes its marketing; legal risk can be real, but rarely the end of the product.

quotes.text: 57 NOVELS FACE BANNING ORDERS
quotes.speaker: The Times

claim: Books that emphasize vice are as dangerous as narcotics and deserve the same legal penalties.
what_happened: Obscenity law narrowed sharply after Roth (1957) and later rulings; mass paperbacks became ordinary.
lesson: Comparing a medium to narcotics is a rhetorical move, not evidence; ask for the dose-response data.

quotes.text: VILE BOOKS AS DANGEROUS AS NARCOTICS, POPE SAYS
quotes.speaker: Pope Pius XII

thing: Jazz, movies, the motor car and sex novels
claim: Jazz, movies, cars and sex novels are making the younger generation wild.
what_happened: The jazz generation grew up to fight WWII and is now remembered as the "greatest generation".
lesson: Every generation's youth panic bundles several new things at once; that bundling is a sign the fear is about change itself.

quotes.text: Jazz, Movies, Motor Car, and Sex Novel Blamed for Wild Youth'
quotes.speaker: Vina Lindsay

claim: Comics, cinema, TV and radio are why a third of 15-year-olds cannot read properly.
what_happened: Literacy rose through the TV era, but heavy TV viewing is associated with less reading time; the displacement half of the fear had some substance.
lesson: Displacement of time is often real even when the bigger harm claim is not; build for the time budget you actually compete for.

quotes.text: Children allowed to see several comics every week, the cinema, television, and radios put the child in a position where there is no need to learn to read
quotes.speaker: Daily Sketch

thing: Lurid magazines, movies and radio programs
claim: Suggestive movies, radio and sex-stimulating magazines are driving a rise in sex crimes.
what_happened: No causal link held up; the same claim moved on to comics (1954), TV, video games and the internet.
lesson: Officials explaining crime by the newest media are rarely right; the blame migrates to each next format.

quotes.text: Liquor, Magazines Blamed For Sex Crimes Increase
quotes.speaker: Walter Hofmann

claim: The telephone is a nerve-wracking nuisance, more trouble than it is worth and not worth paying for.
what_happened: The telephone became universal; even its critics, newspapers included, came to depend on it.
lesson: Early complaints about a product usually describe bad implementation (wiring, service), not a bad idea; fix the rollout and the market appears.

quotes.text: provocative of more profanity than forty prize fights
quotes.speaker: The Times-Democrat

quotes.text: But isn t this too much of a pood thiner The telephone is nuisance nough without this
quotes.speaker: Buffalo Morning Express
quotes.publication: Buffalo Morning Express and Illustrated Buffalo Express

quotes.text: They're a nuisance,
quotes.speaker: Alexander Graham Bell

claim: Constant telephone use causes "telephone ear", a new disease of headaches and lopsided hearing.
what_happened: For ordinary users it never materialized; switchboard operators' noise exposure and headaches were a real occupational complaint (later "acoustic shock").
lesson: Heavy professional users can face real harm that ordinary users never will; size the fear to who is actually exposed.

quotes.text: There is a disease that Is at present quite prevalent in the city
quotes.speaker: The San Francisco Call

quotes.text: If you use the telephone three or- four times a day there is every probability you have.
quotes.speaker: Buffalo Evening News

quotes.text: 'Telephone Ear is A New Malady To Plague The Public'
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: People, and teenagers above all, become addicted to endless telephone talk, a sign of mania or loneliness.
what_happened: Teen phone marathons became a rite of passage with no lasting harm found; by 1996 a columnist called addiction theory "one of the grander social mistakes".
lesson: The "addiction" label gets applied to every new habit of the young; the stronger evidence is what happens to that cohort as adults.

quotes.text: a desire to talk to people at distant points about all sorts of things
quotes.speaker: The Oshkosh Northwestern

quotes.text: In some cases, the expert traces the adolescent's need to talk endlessly on the phone to examples set by similarly addicted mothers
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Addiction theory was one of the grander social mistakes of the 1970s and 1980s.
quotes.speaker: Victoria Advocate

claim: Lovers courting over the telephone are foolish, immoral and a hindrance to business.
what_happened: Phone courtship became normal, and its descendants (texting, dating apps) are how most couples now meet.
lesson: A new channel that people use for romance is a channel people will pay for; the scandal stories are early demand signals.

quotes.text: The telephone is invaluable to love-smitten fools of both sexes
quotes.speaker: Chicago Tribune

quotes.text: the practice of making love over the telephone has proved a serious hindranpe to the transaction of business in the city of Brooklyn
quotes.speaker: The Tribune

quotes.text: lovers ought to know how very unsatisfactory is telephone love.
quotes.speaker: The Joliet Evening Herald-News

claim: A marriage conducted by long-distance telephone cannot be legal because identity cannot be verified.
what_happened: Phone weddings stayed invalid for decades, but remote solemnization arrived: Utah County began licensing video-conference weddings for couples anywhere in 2020.
lesson: Identity verification, not desire, is what holds remote versions of in-person rituals back; the business is in solving verification.

quotes.text: there was too much likelihood of mistaken identity when bride bridegroom are 3000 miles apart.
quotes.speaker: Solicitor Charles E. Wyzanski

quotes.text: Marriages by Telephone Banned
quotes.speaker: Parsons Daily Eclipse

claim: Businessmen using long-distance telephone instead of travelling are killing railway passenger revenue.
what_happened: Telecom did substitute for some business trips, but rail passenger decline came mostly from cars and planes; the same fear returned with Zoom and business travel in 2020.
lesson: Incumbents often spot substitution early and correctly, but misjudge which substitute will do the real damage.

quotes.text: Business men are using it more and more and the way it Is cutting Into our passenger business is a very serious matter to us.
quotes.speaker: S. R. Callaway, president, Lake Shore and Michigan Southern railway

claim: The telephone is demolishing the charming formality of social life, written invitations above all.
what_happened: She was right that formal written invitations faded; most people judged the convenience worth it, as she did herself.
lesson: A critic who says "I could not be happy for a day without it" is describing a cost the market has already accepted.

quotes.text: I am a slave to the phone myself, and I could not be happy for a day without It, but I must admit that it has been largely responsible for the demolishing of all the old, charming formality in our social life.
quotes.speaker: unnamed society hostess

claim: With a telephone a man's house is no longer his castle: it interrupts meals and demands an immediate answer.
what_happened: Interruptions became real, from telemarketing to the do-not-call registry (2003); yet the phone stayed indispensable.
lesson: Always-reachable products win adoption and then breed a second market in blocking and filtering; plan for both.

quotes.text: A Man's House No Longer His Castle If He Has a Telephone
quotes.speaker: Margaret E. Sangster

quotes.text: Undoubtedly the telephone is a great convenience.
quotes.speaker: Margaret E. Sangster

claim: Women ordering food by telephone instead of going to market drives up prices, hides dirty shops and wrecks homes.
what_happened: Phone and later app grocery ordering (Instacart, delivery) became mainstream; food hygiene was solved by inspection rules, not by shopping in person.
lesson: Remote buying is always accused of hiding quality and raising prices; trust and transparency features are what unlock it.

quotes.text: The woman gads about all day and at the last minute rushes to the telephone to order food supplies, instead of going to market,
quotes.speaker: Mrs. John C. Bley, Housewives' League

quotes.text: Don't Order Food by Telephone.
quotes.speaker: Women's Municipal League of Boston

thing: The telephone and the can opener
claim: The can opener and the telephone are killing the art of home baking.
what_happened: Home baking did decline as convenience food and phone ordering spread, and later returned as a hobby; few would call the shift a harm.
lesson: A craft displaced by convenience often comes back as a premium hobby; there is a market on both sides.

quotes.text: Can Opener and Telephone Blamed For Lost Art of Baking in Homes
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: The wireless telephone will be a luxury for the wealthy only.
what_happened: Mobile phones reached most of the world's adults within a century; the cheapest are now the most widespread.
lesson: "Only for the rich" describes the first price point, not the last; plan for the cost curve.

quotes.text: "Wireless Telephone for Wealthy Only"
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Will Rogers predicted seeing someone over the telephone and then dismissed it as something nobody would want.
what_happened: AT&T's Picturephone flopped in 1964, but FaceTime (2010) and Zoom (2020 lockdowns) made video calls ordinary; the dismissal held for about 85 years.
lesson: A dismissal can stay true for decades and still end up wrong; timing is the real question for a product, not whether.

quotes.text: Will Rogers predicts video calling then dismisses it
quotes.speaker: Will Rogers

claim: A member of Parliament called the new transatlantic telephone service a failure.
what_happened: 2,173 calls at $25 a minute in the first year, 90% completed; transatlantic calling became routine and then nearly free.
lesson: Judging a $25-a-minute launch by its volume misreads the curve; the price will fall and the volume will follow.

quotes.text: The transatlantic telephone, recently called a failure by a member of the British Parliament was used from the date of Its opening on Jan. 7, 1927, to Dec. 20 last for a total of 2,173 calls
quotes.speaker: New York Times (reprinted)

claim: Long-distance carriers petitioned the FCC to ban software that lets people talk over the internet without paying for long distance.
what_happened: The FCC declined to ban it; Skype, WhatsApp and FaceTime made long-distance billing nearly obsolete and the petitioners' business model with it.
lesson: When an incumbent asks a regulator to ban a product used by 20,000 people, read it as a signal that the product works.

quotes.text: has petitioned the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to stop several software firms from selling programs that create a voice pipeline between two computers on the Internet.
quotes.speaker: Tom Abate

quotes.text: At the moment, only 20,000 to 30,000 people worldwide are using this new technology.
quotes.speaker: Tom Abate

claim: A pager puts workers on an electronic leash, a reachability that becomes an offensive invasion of privacy.
what_happened: Being always on call became the norm through BlackBerry, smartphones and Slack; "right to disconnect" laws (France 2017) show the harm was real.
lesson: Tools that expand an employer's reach get adopted and then regulated; build in the off-switch before the law demands it.

quotes.text: Being placed on an electronic leash, yankable at any moment, carried reachability to an offensive extreme.
quotes.speaker: William Safire

claim: Teenagers carrying pagers must be drug dealers.
what_happened: Pagers became ordinary teen gear and were then replaced by cell phones that every teen carries.
lesson: When a tool's first visible users are criminals, the stigma lasts only until ordinary users outnumber them.

quotes.text: Not all teen-" 'agers who carry ' pagers are drug dealers.
quotes.speaker: John Fulwider

claim: Cellphones that take photos threaten privacy and must be restricted or banned.
what_happened: Saudi Arabia's 2004 ban failed and camera phones became universal; voyeurism laws (US Video Voyeurism Prevention Act 2004) show the abuse was real.
lesson: A ban rarely stops a capability bundled into a must-have device; the lasting fix is a targeted law against the abuse.

quotes.text: 'Cellphones That Snap Photos Raise Privacy Questions'
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Saudi Arabia bans cellphone Cameras
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: The overland telegraph is the greatest humbug of the year.
what_happened: The transcontinental line opened in October 1861 and connected the coasts for good.
lesson: Calling the newest thing a "humbug" after a run of failed predecessors confuses the fate of the last attempt with this one.

quotes.text: the greatest humbug of 1861.
quotes.speaker: The Placer Herald

claim: The telegraph will kill the Pony Express.
what_happened: The Pony Express shut down in October 1861, two days after the transcontinental telegraph was completed, after only 18 months.
lesson: A business built purely on speed of delivery dies the day a faster channel appears; know which part of your value is speed alone.

quotes.text: The '-Telegraph"' kills the Pony by the lirst electric current breathed across the deserts and the mountains
quotes.speaker: The Placer Herald

quotes.text: The telegraph killed the pony that killed the steam boat.
quotes.speaker: card summary

claim: Faster news does nothing for human happiness; knowing events days sooner is of no consequence.
what_happened: Instant long-distance communication became the backbone of markets, journalism and diplomacy.
lesson: "Why would anyone need it faster?" is a question markets answer quickly and in the affirmative.

quotes.text: How will its uses add to the happiness of mankind? Has the land telegraph done any good? Has it banished any evil, mitigated any sorrow?
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Telegrams can be read by clerks, leaked and forged; a fake telegram could even swing an election.
what_happened: Wire tampering, leaks and forged dispatches were real and recurred with every channel since; telegraphy thrived anyway and privacy rules followed.
lesson: Trust failures in a new channel are real and solvable with authentication and law; they rarely stop adoption.

quotes.text: TELEGRAPH SECRETS VIOLATED (1881)
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Fake Telegram Accused of swinging election (1883)
quotes.speaker: unknown

thing: The telephone (as a music broadcast medium)
claim: Transmitting music by telephone will destroy the concert hall.
what_happened: Broadcast and recorded music grew enormously and live concerts survived; live music revenue now outstrips recordings.
lesson: A remote copy of an experience usually grows demand for the live original rather than replacing it.

quotes.text: The Telephone - Destroyer of the Concert Hall
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Photography may help painters, but it is contemptible as art and cannot show action as well as an artist's pencil.
what_happened: Photography entered museums (MoMA department 1940) and became an art form; painters moved toward what cameras could not do.
lesson: When a machine makes images, the incumbent art form changes rather than dies, and the new tool gets its own artists; build for them.

quotes.text: utterly contemptible as a work of art
quotes.speaker: unnamed writer

quotes.text: The camera does not show action as realistically as the artist's pencil does
quotes.speaker: London Telegraph (reprinted)

claim: Photography feeds vanity: people pay to display flattering, retouched portraits of themselves in public.
what_happened: Self-display became a mass habit (cartes de visite, then selfies); concern about retouching and beauty standards persists with filters and is partly backed by research.
lesson: Vanity is a durable market; the products that last pair self-display with a defensible honesty norm.

quotes.text: This sort of patronage mostly comes from your easy-going young fellows who are blessed with good looks, good clothes, plenty of loose cash and very little to do.
quotes.speaker: unnamed photographer

quotes.text: A little vanity ia pardonable in a pretty woman but when it brings the fair sex to uoh low and vulgar tricks it becomes s sin
quotes.speaker: The Sacramento Bee

quotes.text: There are no more photographs these days, said a fashionable New York maker
quotes.speaker: Portage Daily Democrat

claim: Gangs are pasting the heads of real society women onto nude bodies and selling the photographs.
what_happened: It was real: a St. Louis photographer was tried in federal court in 1892 for mailing such composites; the same abuse returned at scale as AI deepfakes.
lesson: Fake intimate imagery of real people is a harm every image technology enables; build the consent and takedown layer in from day one.

quotes.text: Their methods are to get possession of the photographs of well known and prominent society women and then attach to the head of the picture the photograph of the half or whole of a nude body.
quotes.speaker: The Topeka State Journal

quotes.text: these photographs, which were of nude or partially nude women, had been so made as to appear to he the photographs of certain well-known St. Louis ladles.
quotes.speaker: St. Louis Post-Dispatch

claim: Photography makes obscene images cheap to copy and import by the thousand.
what_happened: The prediction was accurate: every reproduction technology since has mass-produced pornography. The claim that this would corrupt society is contested, and law settled on age and consent limits.
lesson: Assume any cheap media technology will be used for adult content first; decide your policy before your users decide it for you.

quotes.text: underneath a false bottom, upwards of 1,300 obscene photographs.
quotes.speaker: The Leeds Mercury

quotes.text: The City Flooded With Pictorial Depravity by Irresponsible Men
quotes.speaker: St. Louis Post-Dispatch

claim: Amateur snapshooters photographing people without consent are an invasion of privacy.
what_happened: The Kodak era helped prompt Warren and Brandeis's "Right to Privacy" (1890) and later publicity and voyeurism laws; street photography stayed legal and universal.
lesson: Capture technology forces new privacy law rather than being stopped by it; anticipate the law and design to it.

quotes.text: "Is candid photography an invasion of privacy?"
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Amateur Photographers: The Woods Full of Them (Photographing Girls)
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: The Internet would suffer a catastrophic collapse in 1996 because it had outgrown its design.
what_happened: No collapse came; Bob Metcalfe, inventor of Ethernet, literally ate his column in 1997, and capacity kept multiplying.
lesson: Growing pains in a booming network signal demand, and demand funds capacity; even a top expert can mistake a scaling problem for a ceiling.

quotes.text: The Internet has outgrown its design and needs to be fixed
quotes.speaker: Bob Metcalfe

quotes.text: Net pundit keeps promise to eat his words
quotes.speaker: Reuters

claim: Internet use will soon crash, the latest in a once-a-decade cycle of IT hype and letdown.
what_happened: Usage never crashed; the 2000 dot-com bust hit valuations, not users, and adoption went on to about two-thirds of humanity.
lesson: Separate the investment bubble from the usage curve; one can crash while the other keeps compounding.

quotes.text: When Internet use crashes - as it soon will - we will find we have set ourselves up for yet another great disappointment in information technology
quotes.speaker: Dennis F. Galletta

claim: Internet stuff is already boring: a fad the media is ready to drop.
what_happened: The commercial web was just starting; within five years it was reshaping retail, media and finance.
lesson: A media backlash at the start of a curve says the press is bored, not that users are.

quotes.text: 'But no Internet stuff,' she added.
quotes.speaker: unnamed magazine editor

quotes.text: There have been a spate of Internet backlash stories floating through the media in recent weeks.
quotes.speaker: Jim McClellan

claim: The Internet will let investors trade directly with each other and eliminate brokers and the dealer spread.
what_happened: Commissions fell to zero and discount brokers ate full-service ones, but broker-dealers survived by monetizing order flow (Robinhood).
lesson: Disintermediation usually moves the middleman's margin rather than deleting it; find where it relocates.

quotes.text: It's not dumb to ask: Is the brokerdealer business doomed?
quotes.speaker: Bill Barnhart

quotes.text: But in an electronic world, such as the Internet, individual investors can directly match buy-and-sell orders with one another with no spread and no middleman.
quotes.speaker: Bill Barnhart

claim: Ponzi and investment schemes are finding new victims online.
what_happened: The FTC shut down the Fortuna scheme in 1996; online investment fraud became a multibillion-dollar category, peaking with crypto scams.
lesson: Every new financial rail is used for fraud first; trust and verification are features, not compliance overhead.

quotes.text: Ponzi schemes find new pastures on the Internet
quotes.speaker: The Post-Star

claim: Online auction sites let anyone sell anything: kidneys, babies, a killer's art, drugs to teenagers.
what_happened: Abuse was real and forced trust-and-safety teams and prohibited-item rules; online marketplaces still became universal.
lesson: Open marketplaces will be tested by their worst sellers within months; moderation is part of the product.

quotes.text: First it was human kidneys, Then it was babies.
quotes.speaker: Associated Press

quotes.text: FDA investigates eBay drug auction
quotes.speaker: Associated Press

claim: Meeting sexual partners online is spreading AIDS.
what_happened: Studies did link online partner-seeking to higher STI risk in some groups; the same apps later became channels for testing and PrEP outreach.
lesson: A channel that concentrates a risk can also be used to deliver the remedy; partner with health outreach early.

quotes.text: Internet blamed in spread of AIDS
quotes.speaker: The Baltimore Sun

claim: Thinking machines will overtake man and rule the universe.
what_happened: Not true of the machines of 1948, and nothing like it happened in 75 years; the same fear is now argued seriously about AI, so the question is open.
lesson: An existential fear that is early is not necessarily wrong forever; separate "not with this machine" from "never".

quotes.text: 'Lowly Machines to Overtake Man, Rule Universe'
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: "The Thinking Machine.... Friend or Foe?"
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Electronic brains may soon have little to do: there is not enough work for them.
what_happened: Demand for computation has grown without pause for 70 years.
lesson: Demand for a general-purpose capability grows to fill its falling price; don't size the market from today's uses.

quotes.text: 'ELECTRONIC BRAINS MAY SOON HAVE LITTLE TO DO'
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: The abacus is better than a computer because it's so much simpler
quotes.speaker: unknown

thing: Computerized air traffic and flight systems
claim: Computers may create a new danger in air transportation.
what_happened: Automation made flying far safer overall, yet automation-related failures (e.g. 737 MAX MCAS, 2018-19) show the risk was real.
lesson: Automation lowers average risk and creates new rare failure modes; design and disclose for the rare mode.

quotes.text: 'Computer May Create New Danger in Air Transportation'
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Teachers must fight computers that threaten to take over their work.
what_happened: Teacher employment did not fall; computers became classroom tools, and the same fear now attaches to AI tutors.
lesson: Tools that augment a trusted human role tend to be absorbed into it; sell to the professional, not around them.

quotes.text: 'Teachers Must Fight Computers'
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Home computers are a fad like the hula hoop: nobody has worked out what they are useful for at home.
what_happened: The 1984-85 home computer shakeout was real, but the internet supplied the killer app and by 2000 roughly half of US homes had a PC.
lesson: "No one knows what it is for" describes a missing application, not a missing market; a shakeout is not a verdict.

quotes.text: No one has figured out how a computer can be truly useful at home.
quotes.speaker: David E. Sanger

quotes.text: Do We Really Need Home Computers?
quotes.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.

quotes.text: Apple Wizard says computer 'fad' dying
quotes.speaker: Steve Wozniak

claim: Horror stories lurk in PC spreadsheets: hidden errors will drive bad business decisions.
what_happened: Spreadsheets became universal and the errors proved real (JPMorgan's 2012 London Whale model, the Reinhart-Rogoff error).
lesson: Tools that let non-specialists build models spread fast and fail quietly; verification is the product opportunity.

quotes.text: 'Horror Stories Lurk in Spreadsheets of Personal Computers'
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: The Michelangelo virus is a time bomb that will wipe hard disks worldwide on March 6.
what_happened: Michelangelo hit thousands of machines, not the millions forecast, but malware went on to become a vast criminal industry.
lesson: A specific doomsday date usually fizzles while the underlying threat class grows; invest in the class, not the date.

quotes.text: Computer virus a time bomb
quotes.speaker: Neill A. Borowski

claim: Uncrackable encryption in ordinary hands will let criminals and narcoterrorists hide from law enforcement.
what_happened: Strong encryption became the default (HTTPS, end-to-end messaging); criminals do use it, and the "going dark" fight is still unsettled.
lesson: When a government wants a backdoor, the market usually ends up with the strong version anyway; plan for both pressures.

quotes.text: whether regular folks - presumably including international narcoterrorists -should have access to message-encoding systems so crack-proof that the government can't monitor their communications.
quotes.speaker: The Boston Globe

quotes.text: An encryption program has landed its creator in hot water with enforcement authorities.
quotes.speaker: William Bulkeley

claim: The government's Clipper Chip has a back door that lets agencies read encrypted calls and email.
what_happened: The back door was the design: Clipper was built for key escrow, a flaw in it was published in 1994, and the program was abandoned by 1996.
lesson: A product built around a backdoor for the government has to win the public's trust as well as the government's, and Clipper failed on trust.

quotes.text: The Clipper Chip: Big Brother in your computer
quotes.speaker: Nick Gillespie

quotes.text: But it also features a "back door" through which the government can eavesdrop on encrypted communications.
quotes.speaker: Nick Gillespie

claim: What users get with Windows is more computer cost.
what_happened: GUIs demanded more hardware at first, but they became the only way most people used computers.
lesson: A new interface that costs more compute at first wins once hardware catches up; build for the hardware of three years from now.

quotes.text: What Do users Get with Windows? More computer cost.
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: The Year 2000 date bug will crash critical systems; prepare for battle.
what_happened: About $300 billion went into remediation worldwide and very little failed; whether the fear was overblown or the fix worked is still argued.
lesson: A warning that triggers successful prevention looks wrong afterwards; judge it by the cost of the fix against the cost of the failure.

quotes.text: Be Prepared to Battle Y2K
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Riding elevators causes a new disease, "elevator sickness".
what_happened: Elevators became the precondition of the skyscraper city; no elevator sickness beyond brief vertigo was ever established.
lesson: A new motion sensation often gets named as a disease; adaptation usually follows within a generation.

quotes.text: "Cases of elevator sickness are on the increase," said Dr. E. C. Knowlton, of Chicago.
quotes.speaker: Dr. E. C. Knowlton

claim: Automatic elevators will throw elevator operators out of work.
what_happened: The operators' job almost disappeared; ironically, the 1945 New York elevator strike sped up the switch to automatic cars.
lesson: A union strike that shows how much a city depends on a manual job can speed up the automation of that job.

quotes.text: The union fears many of its members may be thrown out of work
quotes.speaker: Elevator Operators Union

quotes.text: Thousands Walk as Strike Ties Up All Rockefeller Center Elevators
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Elevators without operators are unsafe, inviting accidents and even crime, and should be banned.
what_happened: Industry data cited one accident per 140 million riders on automatic cars against five on operated cars; automatic elevators became universal.
lesson: Safety arguments from people whose jobs depend on the old system need checking against accident data; the data often favours the machine.

quotes.text: is only one accident for every 140,000,000 persons transported by automatic type compared to five accidents among the same number of passengers carried by elevators with operato
quotes.speaker: elevator industry

quotes.text: Automatic Elevator Blamed in Part for Crime Rise
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Teddy bears destroy little girls' maternal instincts and will become a major cause of "race suicide".
what_happened: The teddy bear became the most enduring toy of the century; birth rates were driven by economics and contraception, not toys.
lesson: Fears that a toy will rewire a child's nature are almost always wrong; the toy becomes the nostalgia of the next generation of parents.

quotes.text: The priest held that the toy beasts in the hands of little girls were destroying all instincts of motherhood and in the future would be realized as one of the most powerful factors in race suicide.
quotes.speaker: Rev. Michael G. Esper

quotes.text: "School teaches are declaring that the Teddy bear is a menace and must be abolished."
quotes.speaker: school teachers

claim: Mirrors built into everything are breeding a mania of vanity.
what_happened: Mirrors became fixtures of every room and handbag, and by 1919 columnists praised the hand mirror as "an instrument of humility".
lesson: Moral framing flips fast: the vanity object of one decade is sold as self-care in the next.

quotes.text: Mirror Mania
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Contrary to its undeserved reputation as a symbol of vanity, the hand-mirror is, instead, an instrument of humility.
quotes.speaker: The Wichita Beacon

claim: Putting watches everywhere feeds a rabid obsession with time in an age of rush.
what_happened: Personal timekeeping became universal and essential to rail, work and daily life; the complaint returned with smartwatches.
lesson: Products that make a scarce resource (time) visible spread everywhere; the "obsession" is the market.

quotes.text: The watch mania, as it. is called, is certainly excessive; indeed it becomes rabid.
quotes.speaker: The Newcastle Weekly Courant

claim: Manufactured ice is inferior to natural ice, which is free of germs.
what_happened: Natural ice cut from polluted rivers was the real typhoid risk; manufactured ice, then refrigerators, replaced the ice harvest entirely.
lesson: "Natural is safer" from the people who sell the natural version deserves the hardest look; the data often runs the other way.

quotes.text: Natural Ice is Free of Germs
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Artificial Ice Not Inferior
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Canned music will put live musicians out of work.
what_happened: Sound film eliminated most theatre-orchestra jobs within a few years of 1927; the musicians' union later struck against recording (1942-44).
lesson: A technology that replays a performance does destroy the jobs of those paid to perform it repeatedly; the work that survives is what cannot be copied.

quotes.text: Violinist Made Idle by Canned Music
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Murder of Music Laid to Machines
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Recorded music will have a poisonous influence on ordinary people and degrade musical culture.
what_happened: Recording spread classical, jazz and folk to mass audiences and created whole genres; "canned music" became just music.
lesson: Elite fears that cheap access will cheapen culture usually miss the new forms that cheap access creates.

quotes.text: Upper class man worries about poisonous influence of recorded music upon common folk
quotes.speaker: unknown

quotes.text: Recorded music was controversial. The term ‘canned music’ used as epithet
quotes.speaker: Western Daily Press

thing: The pace of modern business life
claim: Modern high-tension living is cutting ten years off men's lives.
what_happened: US life expectancy rose from about 57 in 1928 to nearly 79; chronic stress is real but modern life lengthened lives.
lesson: Claims that modernity shortens lives can be checked against life tables, and the tables usually say the opposite.

quotes.text: They're cutting down their lives an average of ten years,
quotes.speaker: Dr. J. C. Anderson, state health officer

claim: Labour-saving inventions are making this a lazy age.
what_happened: Labour-saving tech freed huge amounts of time and raised living standards, though sedentary lifestyles did bring real health costs.
lesson: Saving labour does cost something (exercise, skills), but people take the trade almost every time; sell the time saved and offer something for what is lost.

quotes.text: A Lazy, Labor-Saving Age
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Light without a wick is impossible.
what_happened: Gas lit London streets within a decade and most cities within decades.
lesson: Incredulity that something can work without the familiar part is usually a failure of imagination, and it doesn't last.

quotes.text: "Do you mean to tell us we can have light without a wick?"
quotes.speaker: critics of William Murdoch
quotes.publication: Light Without a Wick, a Century of Gas-Lighting

claim: The motorized "solo devil wagon" may add new terrors to city streets.
what_happened: The Autoped faded by 1921; shared e-scooters returned in 2018 with real injury spikes and city rules.
lesson: A fear can outlive its product and be right about the successor; city regulation decides which version survives.

quotes.text: "Solo Devil Wagon Taken Up in a Serious Way Might Add new Terrors to City Life"
quotes.speaker: unknown

claim: Textile frames will destroy the livelihoods of skilled knitters, so the Luddites smashed them.
what_happened: The stockingers' wages and status did collapse, but mechanized textiles created far more jobs in total.
lesson: A technology can be bad for its incumbents and good for everyone else at once; plan for both.

quotes.text: the object of the Luddites
quotes.speaker: The Freeman's Journal
